opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what excites me most is AI finally moving out of the purely digital world and into the physical one. For the last decade, most of the breakthroughs have been in bits: language, images, code, recommendations. Those are incredibly valuable, but the physical infrastructure that runs our civilization, like power plants, water treatment facilities, manufacturing lines, and data centers, is still largely operated the same way it was thirty or forty years ago. You have very skilled human operators running these enormously complex systems using rules of thumb, static setpoints, and logic that was programmed once and rarely revisited.

I got a taste of what's possible back when we were working on data center cooling at DeepMind. Even in facilities that were already considered best-in-class, there was a meaningful amount of energy being left on the table simply because no human can reason about hundreds of interacting variables in real time, continuously, around the clock. When you apply reinforcement learning to that kind of problem, the system starts discovering strategies that experienced engineers hadn't thought of, and then it keeps improving.

So over the next five to ten years, I think we'll see a shift from AI as a tool that gives humans recommendations to AI as an autonomous, trusted operator of critical systems, working alongside people rather than replacing them. That has huge implications. Industrial energy use is a massive share of global emissions, so even single-digit percentage efficiency gains, applied at scale, are a very big deal for climate. And it matters for resilience too. A lot of these industries are facing a wave of retirements, and decades of operational knowledge are walking out the door. AI systems that can learn, retain, and build on that expertise could help close that gap.

The hard part, and also the interesting part, is trust. In the physical world, you can't just ship something and fix the bugs later, because mistakes have real consequences. So the next decade is going to be about building systems that are not only intelligent but also safe, explainable, and reliable enough that operators genuinely want to hand over the controls. When we get that right, I think it'll be one of the most impactful applications of AI that most people never actually see.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What excites me most is actually the unglamorous stuff: the industrial world. People tend to think of AI applications as chatbots and image generators, but the biggest economic and climate opportunities are in physical systems that have been running on decades-old control logic. Data centers, chemical plants, power grids, commercial buildings, water systems. These are enormous, energy-hungry machines operated largely by rules written in the nineties, and we now have a tool set that can actually learn how they behave and run them better.

I saw this firsthand at Google, where we used reinforcement learning to help cool data centers. The thing that stuck with me wasn't the efficiency gain itself, it was how transferable the approach turned out to be. Almost every industrial facility is a system with sensors, actuators, a physical model nobody has fully written down, and a human operator making judgment calls under uncertainty. That is exactly the kind of problem machine learning is good at.

So over the next five to ten years, I think the exciting shift is AI going from making recommendations to actually closing the loop, operating equipment in real time, within hard safety constraints, and with humans supervising rather than turning every knob. The cumulative effect of doing that across the built environment is measured in gigawatts and gigatons, not just click-through rates.

The second thing that excites me is that the barrier to deploying this is collapsing. It used to take a team of PhDs a year to stand up one of these systems for one site. The tooling, the models, and the data infrastructure are maturing to the point where it can be done quickly and repeatably, which is what you need to reach the hundreds of thousands of facilities that actually matter.

astra-6.text:
What excites me most is AI’s potential to help us solve problems in the physical world. We’ve made tremendous progress with systems that work with text and images, and I think the next five to ten years will bring more applications that help us operate complex systems—energy infrastructure, manufacturing, transportation—more effectively.

The interesting thing is that even a small improvement in those systems can have a huge impact. If you can use less energy to deliver the same outcome, or make a process more reliable, that value compounds across an entire industry.

But getting there requires more than a capable model. You need systems people can trust, that work within real operational constraints, and that help the people responsible for those decisions. I’m excited to see that whole package come together—to see AI become a practical tool for tackling problems that have been difficult for a very long time.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me most is AI moving from helping us understand the world to helping us improve it. There are so many places where people make difficult decisions every day—how to operate a factory, manage energy, or keep equipment running—and they’re working with more complexity than anyone can hold in their head.

Over the next five to ten years, I think we’ll see AI become a practical partner in those decisions. The exciting part is the feedback loop: you make a recommendation, take an action, observe what happens, and learn. That connects intelligence to measurable outcomes—less energy used, less waste, more reliable operations.

Getting there takes more than a capable model. You need systems people can trust, with clear boundaries and a way to recover when something goes wrong. But if we get that right, we can make expertise available much more broadly. That’s the possibility I find really compelling.
